{{Short description|Numerical algorithm for mortality forecasting}}
{{Use mdy dates|date=August 2012}}
'''The Lee–Carter model''' is a numerical algorithm used in [[mortality forecasting]] and [[life expectancy]] [[forecasting]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.soa.org/library/journals/north-american-actuarial-journal/2000/january/naaj0001_5.pdf |title=The Lee-Carter Method for Forecasting Mortality, with Various Extensions and Applications &#124; SOA |access-date=September 28, 2010 |archive-date=March 7, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190307054148/https://www.soa.org/library/journals/north-american-actuarial-journal/2000/january/naaj0001_5.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref>  The input to the model is a matrix of age specific [[mortality rates]] ordered monotonically by time, usually with ages in columns and years in rows. The output is a forecasted matrix of mortality rates in the same format as the input.

The model uses [[singular value decomposition]] (SVD) to find:

* A [[univariate]] [[time series]] vector <math>\mathbf{k}_t</math> that captures 80–90% of the mortality trend (here the subscript <math>t</math> refers to time), 
* A vector <math>\mathbf{b}_x</math> that describes the relative mortality at each age (here the subscript <math>x</math> refers to age), and
* A scaling constant (referred to here as <math>s_1</math> but unnamed in the literature).

<math>\mathbf{k}_t</math> is usually linear, implying that gains to life expectancy are fairly constant year after year in most populations. Prior to computing SVD, age specific mortality rates are first transformed into <math>\mathbf{A}_{x,t}</math>, by taking their [[logarithms]], and then [[centering]] them by subtracting their age-specific means over time. The age-specific mean over time is denoted by <math>\mathbf{a}_x</math>. The subscript <math>x,t</math> refers to the fact that <math>\mathbf{A}_{x,t}</math> spans both age and time.

Many researchers adjust the <math>\mathbf{k}_t</math> vector by fitting it to empirical life expectancies for each year, using the <math>\mathbf{a}_x</math> and <math>\mathbf{b}_x</math> generated with SVD. When adjusted using this approach, changes to <math>\mathbf{k}_t</math> are usually small.

To forecast mortality, <math>\mathbf{k}_t</math> (either adjusted or not) is projected into <math>n</math> future years using an [[ARIMA]] model. The corresponding forecasted <math>\mathbf{A}_{x,t+n}</math> is recovered by multiplying <math>\mathbf{k}_{t+n}</math> by <math>\mathbf{b}_x</math> and the first diagonal element of S (when <math>\mathbf{U} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{V^*} = \text{svd}(\mathbf{A}_{x,t})</math>). The actual mortality rates are recovered by taking exponentials of this vector.

Because of the linearity of <math>\mathbf{k}_t</math>, it is generally modeled as a [[random walk]] with trend. Life expectancy and other [[life table]] measures can be calculated from this forecasted matrix after adding back the means and taking exponentials to yield regular mortality rates.

In most implementations, [[confidence intervals]] for the forecasts are generated by simulating multiple mortality forecasts using [[Monte Carlo Method]]s. A band of mortality between 5% and 95% percentiles of the simulated results is considered to be a valid forecast.  These simulations are done by extending <math>\mathbf{k}_t</math> into the future using randomization based on the [[standard error]] of <math>\mathbf{k}_t</math> derived from the input data.

== Algorithm ==

The algorithm seeks to find the least squares solution to the equation:

:<math>\ln{(\mathbf{m}_{x,t})} = \mathbf{a}_x + \mathbf{b}_x \mathbf{k}_t + \epsilon_{x,t}</math>

where <math>\mathbf{m}_{x,t}</math> is a matrix of mortality rate for each age <math>x</math> in each year <math>t</math>.

# Compute <math>\mathbf{a}_x</math> which is the average over time of <math>\ln{(\mathbf{m}_{x,t})}</math> for each age:
#;: <math>\mathbf{a}_x = \frac{\sum_{t=1}^{T}{\ln{(\mathbf{m}_{x,t})}}}{T}</math>
# Compute <math>\mathbf{A}_{x,t}</math> which will be used in SVD:
#;: <math>\mathbf{A}_{x,t} = \ln{(\mathbf{m}_{x,t})} - \mathbf{a}_x</math>
# Compute the singular value decomposition of <math>\mathbf{A}_{x,t}</math>:
#;: <math>\mathbf{U} \mathbf{S} \mathbf{V^*} = \text{svd}(\mathbf{A}_{x,t})</math>
# Derive <math>\mathbf{b}_x</math>, <math>s_1</math> (the scaling eigenvalue), and <math>\mathbf{k}_t</math> from <math>\mathbf{U}</math>, <math>\mathbf{S}</math>, and <math>\mathbf{V^*}</math>:
#;: <math>\mathbf{b}_x = (u_{1,1}, u_{2,1}, ..., u_{x,1})</math>
#;: <math>\mathbf{k}_t = (v_{1,1}, v_{1,2}, ..., v_{1,t})</math>
# Forecast <math>\mathbf{k}_t</math> using a standard univariate [[ARIMA]] model to <math>n</math> additional years:
#;: <math>\mathbf{k}_{t+n} = \text{ARIMA}(\mathbf{k}_t, n)</math>
# Use the forecasted <math>\mathbf{k}_{t+n}</math>, with the original <math>\mathbf{b}_x</math>, and <math>\mathbf{a}_x</math> to calculate the forecasted mortality rate for each age:
#;: <math>\mathbf{m}_{x,t+n} = \exp(\mathbf{a}_x + s_1 \mathbf{k}_{t+n} \mathbf{b}_x)</math>

== Discussion ==

Without applying SVD or some other method of [[dimension reduction]] the table of mortality data is a highly correlated multivariate data series, and the complexity of these multidimensional time series makes them difficult to forecast. SVD has become widely used as a method of dimension reduction in many different fields, including by [[Google]] in their [[page rank]] algorithm.

The Lee–Carter model was introduced by [[Ronald D. Lee]] and Lawrence Carter in 1992 with the article "Modeling and Forecasting U.S. Mortality".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lee |first1=Ronald D |last2=Carter |first2=Lawrence R |title=Modeling and Forecasting U.S. Mortality |journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association |date=September 1992 |volume=87 |issue=419 |pages=659–671 |doi=10.2307/2290201 |jstor=2290201 }}</ref> The model grew out of their work in the late 1980s and early 1990s attempting to use [[inverse projection]] to infer rates in [[historical demography]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://escholarship.org/uc/item/76b3712p|title = Reflections on Inverse Projection: Its Origins, Development, Extensions, and Relation to Forecasting|date = June 5, 2003|last1 = Lee|first1 = Ronald}}</ref> The model has been used by the United States [[Social Security Administration]], the US [[Census Bureau]], and the United Nations. It has become the most widely used mortality forecasting technique in the world today.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://gking.harvard.edu/files/lc.pdf|title=Understanding the Lee-Carter Mortality Forecasting Method|access-date=12 April 2023|website=Harvard University|author1=Federico Girosi|author2=Gary King}}</ref>

There have been extensions to the Lee–Carter model, most notably to account for missing years, correlated male and female populations, and large scale coherency in populations that share a mortality regime (western Europe, for example). Many related papers can be found on [http://www.ceda.berkeley.edu/People/rlee.html Professor Ronald Lee's] website.

== Implementations ==

There are few software packages for forecasting with the Lee–Carter model.

* [http://lcfit.demog.berkeley.edu LCFIT] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220418014625/http://lcfit.demog.berkeley.edu/ |date=April 18, 2022 }} is a web-based package with interactive forms. 
* Professor [[Rob J. Hyndman]] provides an [https://robjhyndman.com/software/ R package for demography] that includes routines for creating and forecasting a Lee–Carter model. 
* Alternatives in R include the [https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/StMoMo/vignettes/StMoMoVignette.pdf StMoMo package] of Villegas, Millossovich and Kaishev (2015). 
* Professor German Rodriguez provides [http://data.princeton.edu/eco572/LeeCarter.html code for the Lee–Carter Model] using [[Stata]]. 
* Using [[Matlab]], Professor Eric Jondeau and Professor Michael Rockinger have put together the [https://github.com/mrockinger/Matlab-Longevity-Toolbox/ Longevity Toolbox] for parameter estimation.
